title_en: Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the Economic Contract Law
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Economic Contract Law

(September 17, 1984)

I. Issues Concerning the Confirmation and Handling of Invalid Economic Contracts

When hearing cases involving economic contracts, the first issue to be resolved is the confirmation of the validity of the economic contract. An economic contract confirmed as invalid is not protected by law and has no binding force on either party. However, economic disputes arising from the invalidation of a contract shall be resolved reasonably in accordance with state laws and policies, based on a clear determination of facts and right and wrong.

A. How to Examine Whether a Contract Is Valid

The legal basis for confirming an invalid economic contract is Article 7 of the Economic Contract Law. In practice, determining whether a contract is valid mainly involves examination from four aspects.

1. Examine whether the subject of the contract possesses legal person status.

This mainly refers to examining whether enterprises, institutions, and other economic organizations other than state organs and groups established in accordance with the law possess legal person status. At present, China has no regulations on legal person registration; however, based on other laws and regulations and relevant provisions, a legal person shall at least be an independent economic accounting entity approved by the state and established in accordance with relevant regulations. The Notice on Carrying out the General Survey and Registration of Industrial Enterprises, issued in 1979 by the State Economic Commission, the State Agricultural Commission, and the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, clearly stipulates that all industrial enterprises under ownership by the whole people and collective ownership must undergo comprehensive registration. Pursuant to this provision, any organization that fails to register in accordance with the regulations after the local comprehensive survey and registration, or has applied for registration but has not been approved by the administrative department for industry and commerce, shall be deemed as not possessing legal person status. The Regulations on the Administration of Registration of Industrial and Commercial Enterprises, promulgated by the State Council on August 9, 1982, stipulate that industrial and commercial enterprises must register with the administrative department for industry and commerce; otherwise, they are not permitted to prepare for construction or commence business, or to engrave official seals or sign contracts, etc. Many of the economic contracts currently in dispute were concluded before the issuance of the above-mentioned Notice and Regulations. In determining whether the subject of such economic contracts possesses legal person status, it is necessary to proceed from the actual circumstances, make specific analyses, and treat different situations differently. For contracts concluded by an economic organization that, although not meeting the prescribed formalities before the comprehensive survey and registration of industrial enterprises, was indeed approved for establishment by a higher competent authority, and if there are no other illegal circumstances, they shall generally be treated as valid contracts. If the organization was established without the approval of a higher competent authority, the economic contract concluded shall be deemed invalid.

When examining legal person status, attention shall also be paid to examining the agent qualifications and scope of authority of the person signing the contract on behalf of the principal. Among these: (1) A contract signed under the name of an entity by unauthorized use or fraudulent assumption of the entity's name shall be invalid. (2) Acts beyond the scope of agency authority shall be invalid, except where ratified by the principal before the dispute arose. (3) A contract signed by an agent in the name of the principal with himself or with another person he also represents shall be invalid. If the person signing the contract does not have a power of attorney but holds a letter of introduction from the commissioning entity that explains the situation, he shall be deemed as having agency qualifications.

For contract subjects that are individual industrial and commercial households, specialized households in rural areas, or economic associations, it is necessary to examine whether they have registered and obtained a license in accordance with legal provisions.

2. Examine whether the content of the contract is lawful.

First, examine whether the subject matter of the contract falls within the scope of production and operation prohibited by laws and policies. Second, examine whether the provisions in the contract regarding the quantity, quality, price, and liability for breach of the subject matter violate state plans, regulations, and policies. Third, examine whether the content of the contract violates state interests or public social interests, or whether there are acts to circumvent the law. Fourth, examine whether the content of the contract exceeds the approved scope of business operations. If, at the time of signing the contract, an application had been made to the administrative department for industry and commerce to change or expand the business scope, and after the contract was signed, the business scope was approved by the administrative department for industry and commerce, it may not be deemed as exceeding the business scope.

3. Examine whether the expression of intent of the parties to the contract is genuine.

Pursuant to Article 5 of the Economic Contract Law, it is necessary to examine whether the expressions of intent of the parties during the process of signing the contract are genuine, and whether there is any violation of the principles of equal mutual benefit, consultation on an equal footing, and exchange of equivalents.

4. Examine whether the contract has fulfilled the statutory approval procedures.

If laws and regulations provide that a contract must be reviewed and approved by the competent authority before becoming effective, and the statutory approval procedures have not been fulfilled, the contract does not have legal binding force.

China's economic system reform is deepening, and new situations are constantly emerging. In examining whether a contract is valid, it is essential to act in accordance with legal provisions, conform to current policies, proceed from actual circumstances, and facilitate further invigoration of the economy and opening up to the outside world.

B. Handling of Invalid Economic Contracts

After an economic contract is confirmed as invalid, two aspects need to be dealt with: one is the property consequences caused by the invalid economic contract; the other is the illegal acts in the invalid economic contract.

Property disputes arising from invalid economic contracts shall be handled by the three methods of restitution, compensation, or confiscation as provided in Article 16 of the Economic Contract Law.

When handling specific cases, attention shall be paid to the following three issues:

1. Distinguish between restitution of property and confiscation of property.

Restitution of property is not a punitive measure but a legal means to eliminate the property consequences caused by an invalid economic contract. Confiscation of property is a punitive measure. According to Article 16 of the Economic Contract Law, confiscation of property is only applicable to invalid contracts that deliberately violate state interests or public social interests, because the nature and harmful consequences of such contracts are more serious than those of other invalid contracts, and handling them by restitution alone is insufficient to eliminate the adverse consequences they cause. Article 16 of the Economic Contract Law stipulates: For an economic contract that violates state interests or public social interests, if both parties are intentional, the property already obtained or agreed to be obtained by both parties shall be confiscated and turned over to the state treasury. If the violation is caused by the intention of one party, the intentional party shall return the property obtained from the other party to that other party, and the property obtained or agreed to be obtained from the intentional party by the non-intentional party shall be confiscated and turned over to the state treasury.

Whether to use restitution or confiscation can generally be determined by analyzing the nature of the conduct leading to the invalidity of the contract, the object of the harm, the consequences of the harm, etc. Contracts that violate laws and state policies mainly involve violations of regulations on industrial and commercial enterprise registration, markets, finance, taxation, finance, trademarks, and labor management, thereby interfering with the state's normal economic management order over enterprises. In such cases, the party at fault may have acted with knowledge and intent, or may have done so due to weak legal awareness or lack of legal knowledge, being unaware of relevant laws and policies or not knowing the necessary legal formalities. However, contracts that violate state interests or public social interests are generally entered into with subjective knowledge and intent, with a motive to seek illegal gains, such as entering into a fake economic contract or using an economic contract to engage in speculation, purchasing and selling obscene books, paintings, audio tapes, video tapes, or purchasing and selling substandard drugs harmful to people's health or prohibited goods.

2. Compensation for losses shall be apportioned according to the degree of fault, with each party bearing a corresponding share.

If both parties to an invalid economic contract are at fault, compensation for losses after restitution of property shall be handled in accordance with Article 16 of the Economic Contract Law, which states that "each party shall bear its corresponding responsibility." The so-called "corresponding responsibility" shall not be interpreted as equal sharing of losses or each party bearing its own losses. The parties to the contract shall respectively bear shares of the economic losses proportionate to the primary or secondary nature and severity of their respective faults.

In addition, the liability for invalid contracts shall be distinguished from liability for valid contracts. If a party breaches a valid contract, liability is mainly assumed by paying liquidated damages, compensating for losses, etc. However, liability for an invalid contract shall be resolved in accordance with the principles set forth in Article 16 of the Economic Contract Law. The two types of liability are different in nature and must not be confused. A contract cannot be confirmed as invalid on the one hand, while on the other hand, the parties are held liable for breach of contract.

3. Methods for confirming and handling invalid contracts.

The confirmation and handling of invalid contracts can be done by the following methods:

(1) Invalid contracts may first be confirmed by a written ruling, and then the property disputes between the parties may be resolved through mediation. However, where an economic contract is used for illegal or criminal activities requiring economic sanctions or even criminal liability, mediation shall not be conducted.

(2) For invalid contracts involving confiscation or fines, confirmation and handling must be done by judgment.

(3) For invalid contracts that do not involve confiscation or fines, confirmation and handling may also be done by mediation statement. In the mediation statement, the invalidity of the contract shall be indicated in the part establishing the rights and wrongs, followed by the agreement reached for resolving the property dispute.

II. Issues Concerning Liability for Breach of Economic Contracts

A. How to Determine Liability for Breach of an Economic Contract

After ascertaining the facts of an economic contract case, clarifying the liability for breach of contract of the parties is the basis for resolving the dispute, in accordance with Article 32, paragraph 1 of the Economic Contract Law, which provides that the party at fault shall bear liability for breach of contract. When analyzing and determining liability for breach, two situations shall be distinguished: one is where the breach has not yet caused harm to the other party, in which case only liquidated damages need to be paid to the other party; the other is where the breach has caused harm to the other party and the loss exceeds the liquidated damages, or the contract does not provide for liquidated damages, in which case compensatory damages shall be paid. In the first situation, liability can be determined solely by the existence of fault and breach of contract. In the second situation, liability for breach shall be established from four aspects: (1) There must be an act of non-performance or incomplete performance of the contract. (2) There must be actual property damage. This refers to losses caused by non-performance or incomplete performance of the contract. The calculation of losses must have a basis. (3) There must be fault, i.e., the non-performance or incomplete performance of the economic contract by a party was intentional or negligent. (4) There must be a causal relationship between the act and the damage result. Regardless of the situation, the degree of liability of the parties shall be determined based on relevant laws and policies, whether it is full or partial liability, primary or secondary liability.

B. Liquidated Damages and Compensatory Damages

Liquidated damages refer to a certain amount of money that a party at fault must pay to the other party in accordance with the contract or legal provisions due to non-performance or incomplete performance of an economic contract, regardless of whether the breach causes loss to the other party. Compensatory damages are compensation paid by the breaching party for economic losses caused to the other party. Where the contract provides for liquidated damages, compensatory damages are used to compensate for the shortfall if liquidated damages are insufficient to cover the economic loss. If liquidated damages are sufficient to compensate for the economic loss, no compensatory damages shall be paid. However, if the contract does not provide for liquidated damages, as long as losses are caused, compensatory damages shall be paid to the other party.

Liquidated damages may be either statutory liquidated damages, expressly provided for by regulations (e.g., the Regulations on Contracts for the Purchase and Sale of Industrial and Mineral Products, the Regulations on Contracts for the Purchase and Sale of Agricultural and Sideline Products), or contractual liquidated damages, agreed upon by the parties at the time of signing the contract. If the contract does not contain a clause on liquidated damages, the relevant regulations in effect at the time of signing the contract may be followed. If the relevant regulations do not provide for liquidated damages and the breach has not caused loss to the other party, the matter may be handled appropriately based on the actual circumstances.

Regarding the amount of liquidated damages, it may be determined by agreement between the parties. However, for intentional breach, liquidated damages and compensatory damages shall not be reduced. For negligent breach, consideration may be given to appropriately reducing liquidated damages, but only if the breaching party is truly in economic difficulty, makes a request voluntarily, or has not caused economic loss to the other party. If the matter is adjudicated by judgment, the economic liability shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of relevant regulations or the contract. Liquidated damages shall be calculated up to the date of conclusion of the case by the People's Court.

Article 37 of the Economic Contract Law stipulates that liquidated damages and compensatory damages shall be paid within ten days after liability is clearly established. This refers to payment within ten days from the date on which the arbitration award of the contract arbitration authority or the mediation statement or judgment of the People's Court becomes legally effective.

C. Issues of Liability for Breach of Contract Where the Higher Leading Organ or Competent Business Authority Is at Fault

Article 33 of the Economic Contract Law provides: If an economic contract cannot be performed or fully performed due to the fault of a higher leading organ or competent business authority, the higher leading organ or competent business authority shall bear responsibility for the breaching party's act of breach. The breaching party shall first pay liquidated damages or compensatory damages to the other party in accordance with the regulations, and then the responsible higher leading organ or competent business authority shall handle the matter. This is because the handling of liability for breach of contract shall be conducted between the parties to the contract, not between the higher leading organ or competent business authority of the breaching party and the other party. Therefore, the liability of the higher leading organ or competent business authority cannot be directly pursued.

In addition, economic contract disputes arising from the adjustment of state plans or the closure or suspension of certain enterprises shall be handled in accordance with relevant state regulations on the maintenance and disposition of assets of closed or suspended enterprises.

D. Issue of Continued Performance of the Contract After Handling of Economic Liability

Payment of liquidated damages or compensatory damages is the primary means by which the breaching party assumes economic liability, but the payment of liquidated damages and compensatory damages does not replace the performance of the physical goods or services specified in the contract. Article 35 of the Economic Contract Law stipulates: "If the other party requests continued performance of the contract, performance shall continue." This provision shall be strictly enforced, especially where one party arbitrarily tears up the contract and has the conditions to continue performance.

If certain items in the original contract require modification or supplementation, the parties may renegotiate and then perform in accordance with the new agreement reached by both parties.

III. Issues Concerning the Statute of Limitations

Article 50 of the Economic Contract Law provides that a party to an economic contract applying to the contract management authority for mediation or arbitration shall do so within one year from the date on which it knew or should have known that its rights were infringed. Applications made beyond that period shall generally not be accepted. This is a provision on the limitation period for arbitration, not on the limitation period for litigation.

Currently, China's laws have not yet stipulated a statute of limitations for litigation. In practice, consideration may be given to whether to accept a case based on the conditions for filing a lawsuit set forth in Article 81 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation), especially whether there is a factual basis, and in conjunction with whether the contract itself contains provisions on a time limit for claiming compensation. If the contract dispute occurred a long time ago, or there is no witness or physical evidence, and the facts are manifestly unascertainable, the case may not be accepted. For a contract that provides a time limit for claiming compensation but the lawsuit is filed beyond that time limit, the case shall not be accepted.

IV. Issues Concerning Crimes and Other Illegal Acts in Economic Contract Cases

Crimes and other illegal acts discovered during the hearing of economic contract cases shall be seriously dealt with by different methods depending on the circumstances.

A. Cases requiring criminal liability shall be referred to the public security and procuratorial authorities for investigation and handling respectively.

B. If there are illegal acts in the instant contract case, but the circumstances are obviously minor, the harm is not great, and they do not constitute a crime, and only economic sanctions are necessary, they may generally be handled directly by the People's Court. If disciplinary sanctions are necessary, the matter shall be referred to the unit to which the party belongs for handling.

C. For matters of violations of law and discipline that are not within the jurisdiction of the court, they may be referred to the relevant departments for handling, but judicial suggestions shall also be made at the same time. When necessary, a copy of the judicial suggestion shall be sent to the higher competent authority and relevant departments of the party concerned.
